claims.text: Equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi can be maintained as a single-phase simple solid solution.
The starting CoCrFeNiTi state has a uniform lattice.
The starting state contains few pre-existing dislocation obstacles and minimal low-angle grain boundaries.
The low hardness and strength are primarily caused by an absence of effective dislocation obstacles.
The homogeneous starting state lacks significant local lattice distortions or heterogeneous features.
In the homogeneous state, dislocations glide with minimal hindrance.
Minimal hindrance to dislocation glide produces low work hardening.
Mild thermal cycling or low-level pre-straining can introduce local lattice distortions without causing phase separation.
The perturbation can increase the density of low-angle grain boundaries without causing major microstructural changes.
Localized lattice distortions and low-angle grain boundaries act as dislocation-pinning sites.
The induced heterogeneities obstruct dislocation motion.
The induced heterogeneities promote dislocation interactions, pile-ups, and increased dislocation density.
Greater dislocation generation and accumulation increase the work-hardening rate.
The perturbation will increase the work-hardening rate relative to the untreated state.
The perturbation will increase hardness and strength relative to the untreated state.
The strengthened material will largely retain its favorable plasticity.
The strengthened material will largely retain its favorable machinability.
The untreated CoCrFeNiTi starting state combines high plasticity and machinability with relatively low hardness and strength.
The proposed mechanism applies only while the alloy remains single phase and avoids phase transformation or significant grain growth.
Comparable dislocation density or low-angle-boundary density after treatment would refute the claim that the starting lack of obstacles causes low hardness.

contradictions.description: The stated loading boundary limits testing to the elastic-to-early-plastic regime, whereas ultimate tensile or compressive strength generally requires loading well beyond early plastic deformation.
